mappings.note: Exact duplicate of L138. Single substitution carrying a sign; base numerical.

Two cases must be compared to discover that the deciding factor is momentum and not mass or speed separately - LO-66's key-factor identification, the same treatment as the packaging-materials table O42. The momentum content itself is unhoused.
Duplicate of L159 - conservation of momentum with the third law as the stated principle. Flagged.

Static friction holds the car until the push exceeds it (LO-63), the sub-questions turn on balanced versus unbalanced (LO-62), and the whole case is a real event to be explained (LO-65). All three are separately asked.

A designed comparison with release height held constant so that surface is isolated as the variable - LO-66's key-factor identification on top of LO-63. The controlled-variable design is why this earns LO-66 and the plain friction items do not.
Friction rising to match the push (LO-63), the balanced-then-unbalanced transition (LO-62), and part 4 explicitly asks which law describes the stationary phase, which is the first (LO-5).

The first law in the cleanest possible setting, with the absence of friction and air resistance as the stated reason (LO-63). Part (b) names Newton's first law outright, so LO-5 is graded content rather than background.

Parts 1-3 are inertia and its proportionality to mass (LO-5); part 4 asks which law sets the force needed for equal acceleration, which is the second (LO-6). The case study straddles the two laws deliberately.

Part (a) computes an acceleration (LO-7); part (b) generalises to the inverse proportionality (LO-6). Both are demanded, which is why this carries the pair while the plain numericals carry LO-7 alone.
Cushioning family in case-study form; same outcome pair as the airbag and landing-mat items.
Same pair as the rest of the catching family. The stem's momentum framing has no outcome of its own, so LO-6 is the nearest legal code for it.

Two reaction pairs - block against feet, hands against water - in an everyday event. LO-63 is deliberately not added: neither stem nor answer makes friction the operative force, unlike the walking item O28.
Parts 1-2 are the third law (LO-8), part 3 is a = F/m (LO-6), and part 4 asks about the total momentum of an isolated system, which no outcome covers - C2.1 is cited for that part alone. Flagged.
Recoil explained by equal forces and unequal masses. The same as C187 minus the momentum-conservation part, which is exactly why C2.1 is dropped here.

Part 1 is a balanced-force verdict (LO-62), part 2 is F = ma (LO-7), part 3 adds friction back to recover the applied force (LO-63). All three parts are separately graded, so all three codes are earned.
A described velocity-time graph is analysed phase by phase (C2.1) and each phase converted to a net-force statement (LO-64). Reading rather than drawing, so C2.1 and not C8.1.

The whole point is that weight and the normal force are NOT a third-law pair (LO-8) even though they do balance (LO-62). This is the one item in the chapter where those two outcomes are in tension rather than merely adjacent - S105 poses the same picture and takes LO-62 alone.

The third law extended to non-contact forces, one of which is the mutual gravitational pull between apple and Earth - C2.2's 'connect it to the laws of motion'. O40 stays with magnets and charges and so takes LO-8 alone.

Internal string tensions dropped (LO-62), the external engine force identified, and a = F/M applied to the combined mass (LO-6), with the single-system idealisation as the model (C8.1). The systems topic has no outcome of its own in this frame.
Two classic inertia demonstrations (LO-5) presented as everyday events to explain (LO-65). Part 4 asks what changes if the strike is slow, which is still inertia and not a second-law calculation.
Inertia in a familiar setting, with part 4 on seat belts as the everyday application. Same pair as C194 - the bank's two inertia case studies genuinely share one outcome.

Three of the four parts are momentum - its definition, its SI unit, and the momentum form of the second law - and this frame has no momentum outcome at all. LO-6 is cited only because part 4 asks for the second law. The worst curriculum fit in the chapter.
